article.headline: The Late-Cycle Memory Trade: Second-Tier Chipmakers Step Into the Supercycle's Slipstream
article.lede: Semiconductor memory is undergoing its most violent upcycle in a generation. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have gorged on AI-driven demand for high-bandwidth memory — and in doing so have left a feast of ordinary DRAM and NAND for everyone else.
article.body:
The phrase "memory supercycle" gets applied to almost every upturn in chip pricing, but the current one is structurally different from its predecessors. At its core is HBM — High-Bandwidth Memory, a stacked DRAM architecture that is physically bonded atop AI accelerators like Nvidia's H100 and H200 to deliver the massive data throughput machine-learning workloads demand. Because one HBM stack consumes roughly three times the wafer capacity of an equivalent volume of conventional DDR5, the three companies that dominate global DRAM production — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — have effectively redirected a large share of their fabs toward a single customer class: hyperscale AI infrastructure. SK Hynix alone held a 53% share of the HBM market in late 2025; its entire DRAM, NAND, and HBM output through 2026 is sold out, much of it committed to Nvidia under long-term contracts.

That reallocation has a shadow side. Conventional DDR4 and DDR5 DRAM — the memory that goes into servers, PCs, networking gear, and industrial equipment — is now in structurally tight supply because the three majors are too busy packaging HBM stacks to keep commodity lines full. This is the gap that Taiwan's second-tier players are filling. Nanya Technology (TPE: 2408), Taiwan's second-largest DRAM maker with roughly 60,000 wafers per month of capacity, reported Q1 2026 net sales up 583% year-on-year and a gross margin of 68%, driven by average selling prices that jumped more than 70% quarter-on-quarter alone. The company is late-cycle by design: having sat out the HBM arms race, Nanya now finds itself the reliable supplier of choice for DDR4 in a market where the majors have walked away from the category.

Winbond Electronics (TPE: 2344), which specialises in low-density specialty DRAM and NOR flash for embedded applications — automotive, industrial, networking — returned to full utilisation in late 2025 after four loss-making quarters and has since posted consecutive record revenues. Its Kaohsiung fab is advancing from 25-nanometre to 20-nanometre process technology, expanding available bit-density in a niche that the majors have never contested. Macronix (TPE: 2337), focused on NOR flash for microcontrollers and code-storage applications, occupies an even narrower and more defensible corner: it is sampling 3D NOR flash in the second half of 2026 ahead of full production in 2027, a node transition that should extend its pricing power in markets where NAND is simply the wrong technology.

The NAND side of the ledger tells a parallel story. SanDisk (NASDAQ: SNDK), spun out of Western Digital in February 2025 as a pure-play NAND and SSD business, gained roughly two percentage points of global NAND market share in the twelve months to June 2025 — even as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Kioxia lost share — and its stock rose nearly 560% in 2025 alone. Kioxia Holdings (TYO: 285A), the former Toshiba memory unit that went public in Tokyo in December 2024 at ¥1,455 per share, is advancing long-term supply agreements with hyperscale cloud providers out to 2028 and 2029, as enterprise flash demand from AI inference servers — which industry forecasters expect to account for more than 40% of flash demand by 2029 — keeps the market taut. Persistent speculation about a SanDisk-Kioxia merger of equals has not dissipated following the IPO; the two already share fabrication assets.

The most consequential wildcard is China. Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC, unlisted), China's state-backed NAND champion, has climbed to a 13% shipment share of the global market as of late 2025 and is targeting 15% by the end of 2026, building a new production line using domestically sourced equipment to circumvent US export controls. ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT, unlisted), the state DRAM counterpart, held roughly 11% of global DRAM wafer capacity in 2025 and is projecting nearly 14% by 2027, with Shanghai expansion plants under construction and HBM qualification underway. Both companies are beneficiaries of the same gap the Taiwanese players are exploiting — but they also represent the most significant medium-term threat to pricing discipline, as state subsidy insulates them from the margin pressure that normally disciplines capacity additions.

The tweet's intuition is correct: the supercycle's first act, priced in by the big three, is largely over for momentum traders. The second act — diffusion of pricing power down the supply chain toward specialty and commodity players with lower bases and captive niches — is where the asymmetric opportunity now lives. History suggests these late-cycle beneficiaries catch up with a lag of two to four quarters after the leaders peak. The risk, as ever with memory, is that the lag turns into a hangover: if HBM capacity expansions at Samsung and SK Hynix (M15X operational by mid-2027, P5 by 2028) arrive just as AI capex plateaus, the freed wafer capacity could flood back into commodity DRAM, collapsing exactly the scarcity that has made Nanya's margins possible. For now, the tide is still rising — and a rising tide, in semiconductors, lifts surprisingly small boats.

concepts.definition: A period of sustained above-trend pricing and demand in the DRAM and NAND flash markets, typically driven by a structural shift in end-demand — in this cycle, the build-out of AI data-centre infrastructure — that causes supply to lag demand long enough to push average selling prices sharply higher across the industry.

The two dominant types of semiconductor memory. DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory) is volatile — it loses data when powered off — and used for working memory in CPUs, GPUs, and servers; it is fast but expensive per bit. NAND flash is non-volatile storage — data persists without power — used in SSDs, smartphones, and data-centre storage; it is slower but far cheaper per bit. The two markets cycle independently, though both are currently in an upcycle driven by AI infrastructure spending.

A premium DRAM architecture in which multiple DRAM dies are stacked vertically and connected through microscopic silicon vias, then physically mounted on the same package substrate as a GPU or AI accelerator via a process called 2.5D packaging. The result is memory bandwidth of 4–8 terabytes per second — orders of magnitude beyond conventional DDR5 — at the cost of much greater wafer consumption and manufacturing complexity. HBM is the defining memory product of the current AI infrastructure buildout and is produced at scale only by Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.

Macronix focuses on advanced memory technologies such as 3D NAND and high-density NOR Flash to maintain its competitive position.

ticker_sndk.name: SanDisk Corporation
ticker_sndk.blurb: SanDisk was spun off from Western Digital in February 2025 as an independent pure-play NAND flash memory company. It designs and manufactures NAND-based solid-state drives, flash storage chips, and consumer memory products. The spinoff allowed the market to re-rate the business on semiconductor multiples rather than hardware-manufacturer multiples, contributing to an extraordinary post-spinoff rally driven by the NAND supercycle.
ticker_sndk.recent: Since its February 2025 spinoff, SNDK surged over 2,400% through May 2026, reaching an all-time high above $1,189. Fiscal year 2025 revenue was approximately $7.4 billion, with gross margins expanding to ~36% from the low 20s in late 2024, aided by a shift toward high-margin QLC (quad-level cell) products. Analyst targets range from $975 (Wells Fargo, Equal Weight) to $1,250 (Bernstein SocGen, Outperform). A 247 Wall St. analysis in April 2026 flagged potential overvaluation of ~32% versus peers.
